title: Digital Wallet
summary: Design a digital wallet that holds balances and transfers money between users instantly and safely.
statement: Design a digital wallet service. Users hold balances, top up, send money to each other, and pay merchants. Transfers must be atomic, balances never negative, and every movement auditable. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.
coreFunctionalRequirements: Top up and withdraw via external accounts.

requirementQuestions.question: Must balances be strongly consistent at all times?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Selects between strong and eventual models and shapes conflict handling.

requirementQuestions.question: How many wallets, transfers per second, and what peak?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: What happens to transfers when a shard is down?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

requirementQuestions.question: How are fraud and account takeover handled?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Introduces authentication, authorisation, and privacy constraints that affect the design.

requirementQuestions.question: What audit and retention requirements exist?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines the data model, retention, and storage choices.

requirementQuestions.question: Are multiple currencies and holds supported?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: How many writes per second does the ledger take?
How is data partitioned across shards?
What is the share of cross-shard transfers?

keyDecisions.question: How is money represented?
considerations: Immutable ledger entries with derived balances.
Integer minor units to avoid rounding.

keyDecisions.question: How are cross-wallet transfers atomic?
considerations: Same-shard transfers use a database transaction.
Cross-shard transfers use two-phase commit or a saga with holds.

keyDecisions.question: How is data partitioned?
considerations: Hot wallets such as merchants need special handling.

keyDecisions.question: How are risky transfers detected?
considerations: Rule and model checks on the critical path with latency budget.

keyDecisions.question: How is history served?
considerations: Read model derived from the ledger.

commonMistakes: Updating two balances in separate non-atomic calls.
Hot merchant wallets on one row.
Computing balances by scanning all history on every read.
followUps: How do you handle a merchant wallet receiving thousands of payments per second?
How do you support currency conversion?
How do you reverse an erroneous transfer?
How do you recover from a lost shard?
